newsitem.title: INDIA: India president presses for stable government.
newsitem.headline: India president presses for stable government.

text.p: India's president on Sunday told the country's bickering politicians to prove that a new centre-left alliance would be more stable than its predecessor before he would ask it to form a government.

President Shankar Dayal Sharma made the demand to Congress party president Sitaram Kesri, who met him after the United Front coalition elected a leader to succeed caretaker Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda and staked a claim to form a new government.
Congress politicians said Kesri renewed his party's offer of support for United Front prime minister-in-waiting Inder Kumar Gujral. But the president was apparently not impressed.

"President Sharma has asked the Congress party to show reliable proof that the new government will not be an unstable one," a senior Congress official told Reuters after a meeting of the party's policy-making Congress Working Committee (CWC).

Congress politicians said their leaders were also holding talks with the Tamil Maanila Congress (TMC) party, whose leader G.K. Moopanar was passed over as a United Front candidate for the top job in preference for Gujral.
The TMC subsequently decided against joining a new government but offered to remain a member of the United Front.

The United Front has 178 deputies in the 545-seat lower house of parliament. Congress, which controls 140 deputies, could become numerically stronger than the United Front if Moopanar defected with his 20 deputies.
"Basically, we want to have bargaining strength vis-a-vis the United Front," one CWC member said.
Congress officials said Sharma had asked that Congress and the United Front to establish a mechanism for ensuring that the next government is a stable one.

Kesri's abrupt withdrawal of support for Deve Gowda forced the government to resign on April 11 after it was defeated in a vote of confidence jointly by the Congress and its rightwing Hindu opponent, the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

Earlier on Sunday, parliamentarians from the 15-party alliance elected 77-year-old Gujral as their leader, endorsing the choice made late on Saturday by the coalition's decision-making Steering Committee.
Alliance leader Chandrababu Naidu told reporters he expected Sharma to invite Gujral later on Sunday to head the government.
"We have staked a claim to form the government," Naidu said. "We are hopeful of forming the government very soon."
But Sharma's message to Kesri dampened that hope.

A communist leader said the United Front and Congress were trying to establish a mechanism for ensuring better communication between the two formations, which during Deve Gowda's 10 months in office kept each other at arm's length.

The Press Trust of India (PTI) said the two camps agreed on a 10-member coordination committee, with five members from each side. In the event of differences, the prime minister and the Congress president would meet to try to resolve the problems.
United Front officials said Congress had made at least two other demands, including a say in the future cabinet.

It was not clear whether the new government would be sworn in before parliament reconvened at 11 a.m. (0530 GMT) on Monday to discuss the 1997/98 (April-March). PTI said the speaker of the lower house, P.A. Sangma, had called a meeting of all parties at 9:30 a.m. (0400 GMT) to discuss the budget.
